This case report describes a 37-year-old diagnosed with Alzheimer's who had symptoms including cognitive decline, trouble with purposeful movements, disorientation, and sleep problems. If you are concerned, it is very important to see a neurologist or memory specialist who can perform a thorough evaluation, which may include brain imaging and other tests.

example_qa.q: What is an amyloid PET scan and should my loved one have one?
example_qa.a: An amyloid PET scan is a type of brain imaging that looks for abnormal protein deposits (amyloid plaques) associated with Alzheimer's disease. In this case, it helped confirm the diagnosis in a young patient. Whether this test is appropriate for your loved one depends on their specific situation — your doctor or neurologist is the best person to advise whether it would be helpful in their case.

example_qa.q: My younger relative with Alzheimer's is having a lot of trouble sleeping. Is that normal and what can we do?
example_qa.a: Sleep disturbances are indeed common in Alzheimer's disease, including in younger patients as described in this case. They can be very challenging for both the person with dementia and their caregiver. It is worth raising this with the medical team, as there may be strategies — such as improving sleep routines, adjusting the environment, or in some cases medication — that can help. Taking care of your own sleep as a caregiver is also very important.

summary_text: This 2017 case report describes a 37-year-old man with early-onset Alzheimer's disease who presented with gradual cognitive decline, apraxia, disorientation, and sleep disturbances. Brain amyloid PET imaging using 18F-Florbetaben revealed diffuse amyloid deposits with a notable concentration in the striatum, an unusual pattern that carries specific clinical implications. The case highlights that Alzheimer's disease can occur in young adults and may present with a broader range of symptoms than memory loss alone, including difficulties with purposeful movement and disrupted sleep. Advanced imaging tools like amyloid PET can support earlier and more accurate diagnosis. For caregivers, this case underscores the importance of seeking specialist evaluation when a younger person shows cognitive changes, understanding that sleep and behavioral symptoms are part of the disease, and knowing that modern diagnostic tools can help confirm a diagnosis and guide care planning sooner.
title: A Case Report of a 37-Year-Old Alzheimer's Disease Patient with Prominent Striatum Amyloid Retention.

patient_profile: A 77-year-old Caucasian man with severe (end-stage) Alzheimer's disease. He had significant behavioral disturbances alongside his dementia. Prior to the experimental treatment, his Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) score was 3 out of 30 (indicating very severe impairment) and his Functional Assessment Staging Test (FAST) score was 7 (the most advanced stage).
symptoms_behavior: The patient was described as being in a 'stuporous state' — meaning he was largely unresponsive and had extremely limited awareness of his surroundings. He also had significant behavioral disturbances, which are common in advanced Alzheimer's and can include agitation, confusion, and difficulty responding to caregivers.
communication: Not detailed. Given his MMSE score of 3 and stuporous state, meaningful verbal communication was likely severely limited or absent at the time treatment began.
progression: The patient was at end-stage (FAST score 7) Alzheimer's disease at the start of the case. Following the addition of an experimental enzyme called deoxyribonuclease I (DNase I) to his existing memantine treatment, he showed rapid improvement within just 2 days. After 2 months, his MMSE improved from 3 to 18 and his FAST score improved from 7 to 4, suggesting a meaningful, though still impaired, level of functioning was regained.
treatment_management: The patient was already taking memantine, a medication commonly used to manage moderate-to-severe Alzheimer's symptoms. Doctors then added deoxyribonuclease I (DNase I), an experimental enzyme treatment, with informed consent obtained from family members. This is a single case report from 2016 and DNase I is not a standard or approved Alzheimer's treatment. Caregivers should discuss any questions about emerging treatments with the patient's medical team.
caregiver_insights: Family caregivers can play a vital role in medical decision-making — in this case, family members gave informed consent for the experimental treatment on behalf of a patient who could not do so himself. Knowing your loved one's wishes in advance helps in these moments.
Even in very advanced Alzheimer's, medical teams may sometimes try additional treatments. It is okay to ask the doctor what options exist and what the goals of any new treatment are.

Behavioral disturbances (like agitation or unresponsiveness) in late-stage Alzheimer's are distressing to witness. Keeping the care team informed about changes in behavior — even small ones — helps them adjust the care plan.

This case is a single report of an experimental therapy and should not be taken as a recommendation. Always consult a qualified healthcare professional before considering any new or experimental treatment for your loved one.

example_qa.q: My mom is in late-stage Alzheimer's and barely responds to us. Is there anything that can still help her?
example_qa.a: Late-stage Alzheimer's is very hard for families. While options become more limited, palliative and comfort-focused care can still greatly improve quality of life. There are also researchers exploring new treatments. The best step is to have an honest conversation with her doctor about what goals of care make sense for her now — whether that is comfort, maintaining function, or both.

example_qa.q: I heard about a new enzyme treatment for Alzheimer's. Should I ask about it for my dad?
example_qa.a: It is great that you are staying informed. Some experimental treatments show promise in early case reports, but a single case study is a very early and limited form of evidence. It does not mean the treatment is proven safe or effective for everyone. Share what you have read with your dad's doctor, who can help you understand whether it might be appropriate or available, and what the risks and unknowns are.

example_qa.q: How do doctors decide what stage of Alzheimer's someone is in?
example_qa.a: Doctors use tools like the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE), which tests memory and thinking, and the Functional Assessment Staging Test (FAST), which looks at how well a person can carry out daily activities. Together, these help paint a picture of where someone is in their Alzheimer's journey and guide decisions about care and treatment.

summary_text: This 2016 case report describes a 77-year-old man with end-stage Alzheimer's disease who was in a near-unresponsive state with an MMSE score of 3 and FAST score of 7, already being treated with memantine. With family consent, doctors added an experimental enzyme treatment called deoxyribonuclease I (DNase I). Within 2 days the patient showed notable improvement, and after 2 months his MMSE had risen to 18 and his FAST to 4 — a striking change, though he remained impaired. For family caregivers, this case highlights the important role families play in consenting to treatment decisions for loved ones who can no longer do so themselves, the value of staying engaged with the care team about emerging options, and the need for caution when evaluating experimental therapies that have only been reported in a single case. Behavioral changes and functional decline in advanced dementia should always be communicated to clinicians, who can guide appropriate next steps.
title: Effect of deoxyribonuclease I treatment for dementia in end-stage Alzheimer's disease: a case report.

patient_profile: 78-year-old right-handed African-American woman with moderate-stage mixed dementia (Alzheimer's disease combined with cerebrovascular disease) and a left orbitofrontal brain lesion. She presented with worsening memory and significant behavioral and psychological symptoms of dementia (BPSD).
symptoms_behavior: The patient continuously vocalized her son's name and made repetitive grunting noises throughout her evaluation. These vocalizations were linked to increased anxiety and agitation. Her behaviors caused significant distress to her family caregivers.
communication: The patient's primary verbal output consisted of repetitive vocalization — calling out her son's name and making grunting sounds. She was not communicating in typical conversational language during the evaluation, suggesting her verbal expression was driven by anxiety and agitation rather than intentional communication.
progression: The patient was at a moderate stage of mixed dementia. The case does not provide a detailed timeline of decline, but the presenting concern was worsening memory alongside escalating behavioral symptoms that were distressing to the family.
treatment_management: A nonpharmacological 'redirection' technique was used during the clinical visit and achieved an immediate reduction in vocalizations. The clinical team provided psychoeducation to the family caregivers so they could use the same redirection technique at home. The report notes that psychotropic medications are generally not effective for 'negative' BPSD symptoms like vocalization and may reduce quality of life, making nonpharmacological approaches the preferred first-line treatment.
caregiver_insights: Repetitive vocalizations (calling out names, making sounds) are a recognized symptom of dementia — not intentional behavior — and are often linked to anxiety or agitation.

Redirection, a technique that gently guides the person's attention away from the distressing behavior toward something calming or familiar, can quickly reduce vocalizations and is something caregivers can learn to use at home.
Nonpharmacological approaches like redirection should be tried first before turning to medications, as medications often do not help these types of symptoms and can have side effects.

If a loved one's vocalizations or other behaviors are causing you significant distress, ask the care team for psychoeducation — learning specific techniques can make a meaningful difference in day-to-day caregiving.

example_qa.q: My mother keeps calling out my brother's name over and over. Is this a dementia symptom and what can I do?
example_qa.a: Yes, repetitive vocalization — including calling out a family member's name — is a recognized behavioral symptom of dementia, often connected to anxiety or agitation. A technique called 'redirection' can help: gently guide her attention toward a calming activity, a familiar object, or a soothing sound or topic. Ask your care team to walk you through how to use redirection at home, as it has been shown to reduce these behaviors quickly.

example_qa.q: Should I ask the doctor for medication to stop the constant vocalizations?
example_qa.a: It is worth having that conversation with the doctor, but research suggests that medications are often not very effective for repetitive vocalizations and similar behaviors, and they can sometimes reduce a person's quality of life. Nonpharmacological strategies like redirection are generally recommended as the first step. Your care team can help you weigh the options based on your loved one's specific situation.

example_qa.q: The constant noise is exhausting me. What support is available for caregivers dealing with this?
example_qa.a: Caregiver distress from repetitive vocalizations is very real and very common. Ask the care team about caregiver psychoeducation — learning techniques like redirection not only helps your loved one but can also reduce your own stress. Support groups, respite care, and counseling are also valuable resources. You do not have to manage this alone.

summary_text: This 2014 case report describes a 78-year-old African-American woman with moderate-stage mixed Alzheimer's and cerebrovascular dementia who presented with worsening memory and distressing behavioral symptoms, particularly repetitive vocalization — constantly calling out her son's name and making grunting noises linked to anxiety and agitation. Her family caregivers were significantly distressed. A nonpharmacological redirection technique was used during her evaluation and immediately reduced the vocalizations. Caregivers were then taught to use this technique at home. The case highlights that repetitive vocalizations are a recognized 'negative' behavioral and psychological symptom of dementia (BPSD), that medications are generally ineffective for these symptoms and may harm quality of life, and that redirection and other nonpharmacological strategies should be the first-line approach. For family caregivers, the key practical message is that learning redirection and other behavior management techniques — ideally through caregiver psychoeducation offered by the care team — can meaningfully reduce both the patient's distress and the caregiver's own burden.
title: Vocalization in dementia: a case report and review of the literature.

patient_profile: Three patients with Alzheimer's disease (AD) at a severe stage, all exhibiting significant cognitive decline along with serious Behavioral and Psychological Symptoms of Dementia (BPSD). Specific ages and sexes are not detailed in the report, but all three had advanced symptoms including urinary incontinence and wandering in two of the three cases.
symptoms_behavior: All three patients showed irritability, agitation, anxiety, and apathy. Two patients also experienced urinary incontinence and wandering. Cognitive decline was described as very severe, with one patient scoring 12 out of 30 on the MMSE (a score that indicates severe impairment).
communication: Not detailed in this report, though two patients who had stopped recognizing family members were later able to recognize them again after turmeric treatment, suggesting some improvement in social awareness and connection.
progression: All three patients were at a severe stage of Alzheimer's disease at the time of the report. Over the 12-week treatment period, behavioral symptoms improved significantly. Over approximately one year of continued turmeric use, symptoms did not return (no re-exacerbation of BPSD). One patient's MMSE score improved by 5 points (from 12 to 17 out of 30).
treatment_management: All three patients were given turmeric powder capsules as a supplement alongside their existing care. No specific doses are provided in this summary. After 12 weeks, caregiver burden scores and symptom severity scores on the Neuro-Psychiatric Inventory dropped meaningfully. No adverse reactions were reported in clinical symptoms or laboratory tests. Treatment continued for over one year with sustained benefit.
caregiver_insights: Behavioral symptoms like agitation, irritability, and wandering can sometimes improve with complementary approaches — this case report suggests turmeric supplementation may help reduce BPSD, though it is important to discuss any new supplement with a doctor first.

Caregiver burden was measurably reduced after 12 weeks of turmeric treatment in these cases, reminding us that when a loved one's behavioral symptoms improve, caregiving can become less exhausting and stressful.

Even patients with severe Alzheimer's may show meaningful improvements — two patients who no longer recognized family members regained that ability within a year, which can be deeply meaningful for families.

Turmeric appeared safe in these three cases with no reported side effects, but caregivers should always consult a healthcare professional before starting any new supplement, as interactions with other medications are possible.

example_qa.q: I've heard turmeric might help with my mom's agitation and wandering — is there any evidence for this?
example_qa.a: There is a small amount of early evidence, including this case report of three people with Alzheimer's whose agitation, irritability, and wandering improved after taking turmeric powder capsules for 12 weeks. However, this is just three cases, so it's not conclusive. It's worth bringing up with your mom's doctor, who can help weigh the potential benefits and any risks given her specific medications and health situation.

example_qa.q: Could turmeric improve my loved one's ability to recognize me again?
example_qa.a: In this case report, two patients who had stopped recognizing family members were able to do so again after about a year of turmeric treatment. That said, every person with Alzheimer's is different, and we can't promise the same result. It's an encouraging finding worth discussing with a healthcare provider as part of a broader care plan.

example_qa.q: Is turmeric safe for someone with Alzheimer's who is already on other medications?
example_qa.a: In these three reported cases, turmeric capsules caused no adverse effects in symptoms or lab results. However, turmeric can interact with certain medications, such as blood thinners, so it's very important to check with your loved one's doctor or pharmacist before adding any supplement to their routine.

summary_text: This 2012 case report describes three patients with severe Alzheimer's disease and significant Behavioral and Psychological Symptoms of Dementia (BPSD), including irritability, agitation, anxiety, apathy, wandering, and urinary incontinence. All three patients were treated with turmeric powder capsules, a traditional Indian remedy, and showed notable improvements in behavioral symptoms within 12 weeks, with no adverse reactions reported. Caregiver burden scores dropped significantly during this period. Over approximately one year of continued treatment, symptoms did not return, and two patients who had previously lost the ability to recognize family members regained that ability. One patient also showed a 5-point improvement on the MMSE cognitive test. While this is a very small case series and not a controlled trial, it offers encouraging, caregiver-relevant insights: behavioral symptoms may be addressable through complementary approaches, caregiver burden can decrease when a loved one's behavior improves, and even patients at severe stages can show meaningful gains. Caregivers interested in turmeric supplementation should always consult their loved one's healthcare team first to ensure safety and compatibility with existing treatments.
title: Effects of turmeric on Alzheimer's disease with behavioral and psychological symptoms of dementia.

patient_profile: A 62-year-old woman of Western European descent diagnosed with early-onset Alzheimer's disease (EOAD). Her memory problems began around age 59. She carries a high-risk genetic profile, including a rare PSEN1 gene variant (p.R358P), an APOE ε4/ε4 genotype (a well-known Alzheimer's risk factor), and another variant in the SORL1 gene. She also has a family history of Alzheimer's disease.
symptoms_behavior: She presented with memory impairment starting at age 59, and testing showed problems across multiple areas of thinking and cognition (multidomain cognitive impairment). Brain imaging (PiB-PET and FDG-PET scans) confirmed changes consistent with Alzheimer's disease, including amyloid protein buildup and reduced brain activity in affected areas.
communication: Not detailed in this report. The case focuses on genetic and laboratory findings rather than day-to-day communication abilities.
progression: Symptoms began at age 59 with memory impairment, and by age 62 she had multidomain cognitive impairment confirmed by clinical assessment and brain imaging. This represents an early-onset presentation, meaning dementia developed before the typical age of 65. The speed of decline between these time points is not described in detail.
treatment_management: No specific medications or therapies are described in this report. The case centers on genetic diagnosis and laboratory research to classify a newly identified gene variant. Genetic counseling would be highly relevant for this patient and her family, given the inherited nature of the PSEN1 variant and the positive family history.
caregiver_insights: Early-onset Alzheimer's (starting before age 65) can run in families due to inherited gene changes like PSEN1 variants. If your loved one was diagnosed young, asking a doctor about genetic counseling can help other family members understand their own risk.

A diagnosis of early-onset Alzheimer's may take longer to reach because it is less expected in younger people. Brain imaging and genetic testing, as used in this case, can be important tools for getting a clear answer.

Even when a genetic variant is found, scientists sometimes need more evidence before they can say for certain it causes disease. This does not mean the diagnosis is wrong — it means research is still ongoing and the clinical picture matters greatly.

Caring for someone with early-onset Alzheimer's often brings unique challenges, such as the person still being in the workforce or raising children. Connecting with support groups specifically for early-onset families can be especially helpful.

example_qa.q: My mother was diagnosed with Alzheimer's in her early 60s. Could it be genetic, and should our family get tested?
example_qa.a: Early-onset Alzheimer's (before age 65) is more likely to have a genetic component than late-onset cases. Genes like PSEN1, PSEN2, and APP can be involved. It is a good idea to talk with a doctor or genetic counselor who can review your family history and discuss whether genetic testing makes sense for family members. They can also help you understand what a positive or uncertain result would mean for each person.

example_qa.q: What does it mean when a doctor says a gene variant found in my relative is of 'uncertain significance'?
example_qa.a: A variant of uncertain significance (VUS) means scientists have found a change in a gene but do not yet have enough evidence to say definitively whether it causes disease or is harmless. It does not mean the diagnosis is wrong — doctors still use symptoms, brain scans, and other tests to guide care. Over time, as more research is done, the classification of a VUS can change. Ask your loved one's doctor or a genetic counselor to explain what this specific finding means for your family.

example_qa.q: How is early-onset Alzheimer's different from the more common form, and does it change how we should care for our loved one?
example_qa.a: Early-onset Alzheimer's develops before age 65 and is more likely to be linked to inherited gene changes, though the symptoms and progression are generally similar to the more common late-onset form. Because it strikes during working years, it can affect employment, finances, and parenting roles in ways that differ from older patients. Care strategies are largely the same — focusing on safety, routine, emotional support, and working with a medical team — but connecting with resources specifically designed for younger-onset families can make a real difference.

summary_text: This 2026 case report describes a 62-year-old woman of Western European descent with early-onset Alzheimer's disease (EOAD), whose memory problems began at age 59 and progressed to multidomain cognitive impairment by the time of her clinical evaluation. She carries a newly identified PSEN1 gene variant (p.R358P), an APOE ε4/ε4 genotype, a SORL1 gene variant, and has a positive family history of Alzheimer's disease — a combination that strongly points to a genetic basis for her condition. Brain imaging with PiB-PET and FDG-PET confirmed findings consistent with Alzheimer's. The researchers used laboratory cell models to show that this PSEN1 variant alters the processing of amyloid-beta protein in a way that resembles other disease-causing PSEN1 variants, supporting its likely role in causing disease, though it remains officially classified as a 'hot variant of uncertain significance' pending more family data. For caregivers, the key messages are: early-onset Alzheimer's can be hereditary, genetic counseling is valuable for the whole family, and uncertain genetic findings do not undermine a clinical diagnosis. Day-to-day communication abilities and specific treatment regimens are not described in this report.
title: Clinical and functional evidence supporting the pathogenicity of the novel PSEN1 p.R358P variant in early-onset Alzheimer's disease.

patient_profile: The case report discusses Alzheimer's disease (AD) patients — primarily older adults — who underwent an experimental surgical procedure called deep cervical lymphatic-venous anastomosis (LVA). The patients had progressive cognitive decline characteristic of AD, with comorbidities including age-related degeneration of the brain's lymphatic clearance system. One reported case experienced serious complications: intraventricular hemorrhage (bleeding in the brain), suspected reactivation of Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), and TBA-positive epilepsy (seizures) following the surgery.
symptoms_behavior: Patients presented with the typical features of Alzheimer's disease: progressive memory loss, cognitive deterioration, behavioral abnormalities, and significant difficulty with daily activities. The paper also documents serious post-surgical symptoms in at least one patient, including brain bleeding (intraventricular hemorrhage), seizures (epilepsy), and signs of viral reactivation — all serious complications rather than standard dementia symptoms.
communication: Not detailed in the case text regarding the patient's own communication style or language characteristics. The review focuses on surgical outcomes and safety concerns rather than individual patient communication.
progression: The case involves patients with established, progressive Alzheimer's disease. The review notes that AD follows a chronic, progressive course — with CSF production potentially declining to 50% of normal by middle to late stages. The specific patient who experienced complications showed serious adverse events in the postoperative period, underscoring that the disease and its experimental treatments carry significant and unpredictable risks over time.
treatment_management: The experimental intervention described is deep cervical lymphatic-venous anastomosis (LVA) — a microsurgery originally developed for lymphedema that some clinicians are now applying to AD, theorizing it may help drain harmful proteins (amyloid-beta and tau) from the brain. Standard AD medications mentioned include cholinesterase inhibitors and NMDA receptor antagonists (such as memantine), which can temporarily ease symptoms but do not stop disease progression. The review strongly cautions that LVA's safety and efficacy in AD are unproven, and that at least one patient suffered severe complications: brain hemorrhage, possible viral reactivation, and seizures. The authors call for rigorous clinical trials before wider use.
caregiver_insights: This experimental surgery (LVA) is not a proven or approved treatment for Alzheimer's disease — if a family member is offered it, it's important to ask detailed questions and seek a second opinion from a specialist before agreeing.

Serious complications including brain bleeding and seizures have been reported after this surgery in AD patients, so the risks are real and significant, especially for elderly or medically fragile loved ones.

Current standard medications for Alzheimer's (such as cholinesterase inhibitors) can help manage symptoms temporarily but do not cure or stop the disease — caregivers should have honest conversations with doctors about realistic expectations.

Be cautious of clinics or hospitals promoting LVA as a 'breakthrough' for Alzheimer's — as of 2025, the scientific evidence is still very limited, and many early reports have small numbers of patients and very short follow-up periods.

example_qa.q: I heard about a new surgery to drain toxins from the brain in Alzheimer's. Is it safe for my mother?
example_qa.a: This surgery, called lymphatic-venous anastomosis (LVA), is still experimental for Alzheimer's disease. A published review found that at least one patient experienced serious complications including bleeding in the brain and seizures after the procedure. The evidence that it works is very limited, and no large, rigorous clinical trials have been completed yet. It's very important to talk with your mother's neurologist and possibly seek a second opinion before considering any experimental surgery.

example_qa.q: Why don't the current Alzheimer's medications stop the disease from getting worse?
example_qa.a: The medications currently approved for Alzheimer's — such as cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine — help manage symptoms like memory loss and confusion for a period of time, but they don't address the underlying buildup of harmful proteins in the brain. Researchers are actively working on new treatments, but as of now, no medication has been shown to fully stop or reverse Alzheimer's progression. Your loved one's doctor can help you understand which medications might offer the most benefit at their current stage.

example_qa.q: What should I ask a doctor if they suggest an experimental treatment for my family member with Alzheimer's?
example_qa.a: Great questions to ask include: Has this treatment been tested in a proper clinical trial with a control group? What are the known risks and complications? How many patients have received this treatment and what happened to them long-term? Is this treatment approved by a regulatory body? Are there other options? Getting answers to these questions — and possibly a second opinion — can help you make a more informed and safe decision for your loved one.

summary_text: This 2025 review and case report examines an experimental surgical procedure — deep cervical lymphatic-venous anastomosis (LVA) — being offered to Alzheimer's disease patients in China and elsewhere, based on the theory that improving the brain's lymphatic drainage system could help clear harmful proteins like amyloid-beta and tau. The paper describes at least one AD patient who suffered severe post-surgical complications including intraventricular hemorrhage (bleeding in the brain's ventricles), suspected reactivation of Epstein-Barr virus, and epilepsy (seizures). The authors — neurologists and neurosurgeons — conclude that the scientific evidence for LVA in AD is extremely limited, with only small, short-term, non-randomized studies available and no proven efficacy. Despite this, over 380 hospitals in China had already begun offering the procedure by 2025. For family caregivers, the key takeaway is that this surgery carries serious, documented risks and has not been validated in rigorous clinical trials; standard treatments like cholinesterase inhibitors remain the evidence-based option for symptom management, and any offer of experimental surgery should be carefully scrutinized with a trusted specialist.
title: Intraventricular hemorrhage, suspected EBV reactivation, and TBA-positive epilepsy after deep cervical lymphovenous anastomosis in Alzheimer's disease: a case report.

patient_profile: 62-year-old man diagnosed with Sneddon syndrome (SS) associated with antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) — a rare neurocutaneous (affecting nerves and skin) disorder. No specific dementia subtype is named, but he developed significant cognitive decline over a 10-year period.
symptoms_behavior: Initial symptoms included seizures and ischemic (stroke-like) brain lesions seen on MRI, along with a distinctive skin mottling pattern called livedo racemosa. Over 10 years, he developed progressive cognitive decline, additional brain lesions, and worsening skin changes.
communication: Not detailed
progression: The case followed this man over 10 years. His condition gradually worsened despite receiving appropriate medical treatment, with increasing brain lesions on MRI and ongoing cognitive decline — illustrating that SS with APS can progress even when managed.
treatment_management: The report notes he received 'adequate therapy,' though specific medications are not detailed in the summary. In SS and APS, treatment typically involves blood-thinning (anticoagulant) medications to prevent further strokes. Despite this, progression still occurred, highlighting the importance of close medical monitoring.
caregiver_insights: Cognitive decline in conditions like Sneddon syndrome can progress slowly over many years, so caregivers should be prepared for gradual changes in memory and thinking rather than sudden declines.
Even when a loved one is on appropriate treatment, the disease may still progress — this is not a failure of care, and continuing close follow-up with specialists remains important.

Skin changes (mottled, net-like skin discoloration) alongside cognitive symptoms may point to an underlying vascular condition — caregivers who notice both types of changes together should mention this to the doctor.
Regular brain imaging (MRI) and neurological check-ups are important in vascular-related cognitive conditions to track changes and adjust care plans as needed.

example_qa.q: My loved one has a rare syndrome causing both skin changes and memory problems. Why does their cognition keep declining even though they are on medication?
example_qa.a: Some vascular brain conditions, like Sneddon syndrome, can continue to progress slowly over time even with the best available treatments. This is a known challenge with certain rare disorders, and it does not mean the treatment is failing or that caregiving is inadequate. Staying in close contact with the medical team and keeping up with regular check-ups is the most important thing you can do.

example_qa.q: What kinds of cognitive changes should I watch for if my family member has a condition involving small strokes in the brain?
example_qa.a: You might notice gradual changes in memory, difficulty concentrating, slowed thinking, trouble finding words, or changes in mood and behavior. Because these changes can be subtle at first, keeping a simple diary of things you notice — and sharing it with the doctor — can be very helpful for tracking progression over time.

example_qa.q: Is it normal to feel discouraged when my loved one's condition worsens despite treatment?
example_qa.a: Absolutely, and your feelings are completely valid. Watching a loved one decline despite doing everything right is one of the hardest parts of caregiving. Connecting with a support group for caregivers of people with rare neurological or dementia-related conditions can provide both emotional support and practical advice from others in similar situations.

summary_text: This case report follows a 62-year-old man with Sneddon syndrome (SS) and antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) — a rare vascular disorder affecting both skin and brain — over 10 years. He initially presented with seizures and ischemic brain lesions, and over time developed progressive cognitive decline and worsening brain changes on MRI, despite receiving appropriate treatment. While SS is not a common form of dementia, this case is relevant to caregivers because it illustrates how vascular brain conditions can lead to slowly progressive cognitive decline that continues even with proper medical management. Caregivers should be aware that gradual worsening does not indicate a failure of care, and that regular specialist follow-up, brain imaging, and attentive monitoring of both cognitive and physical symptoms are key components of supporting someone with a vascular-related cognitive condition.
title: Long-term clinical progression of Sneddon syndrome associated with antiphospholipid syndrome.

patient_profile: Two Colombian patients with frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD) caused by novel GRN (progranulin) gene variants. Case 1: 42-year-old individual with a predominantly amnestic (memory-focused) presentation, carrying the GRN c.21G>A variant. Case 2: 62-year-old individual with semantic (language/word-meaning) impairment, carrying the GRN c.1098T>A variant. Both were initially thought to have early-onset Alzheimer's disease before genetic and biomarker testing clarified the FTLD diagnosis.
symptoms_behavior: Case 1 showed prominent memory problems resembling Alzheimer's disease. Case 2 had difficulty understanding word meanings and semantic knowledge — a pattern called semantic impairment. Both presentations are unusual for FTLD, which more typically causes personality or behavioral changes, making these cases particularly challenging to diagnose correctly.
communication: Case 2 had notable semantic impairment, meaning difficulty understanding or using word meanings — a language-related symptom. Case 1's communication characteristics beyond memory difficulties are not detailed in the report.
progression: Case 1 had symptom onset at age 42 and Case 2 at age 62, both considered early-onset presentations. Brain imaging showed asymmetric temporal lobe atrophy (shrinkage on one side more than the other). The full longitudinal progression over time is not detailed, though the report notes that serial clinical monitoring was important for reaching the correct diagnosis.
treatment_management: Specific medications or therapies are not detailed in this report. The key management emphasis is on an integrative diagnostic approach: combining repeated clinical evaluations, neuropsychological testing, brain imaging, genetic testing, and biomarker analysis. This thorough workup was essential to distinguish FTLD from Alzheimer's disease and guide appropriate care planning.
caregiver_insights: FTLD caused by GRN gene variants can look very similar to Alzheimer's disease at first — memory problems or language difficulties may appear early, so an initial AD diagnosis does not always tell the full story.

Genetic testing can be valuable, especially when dementia starts at a younger age (under 65) or when there is a family history of dementia. Ask the care team whether genetic counseling is appropriate.

Brain imaging and biomarker tests (like cerebrospinal fluid or PET scans) can help doctors distinguish between different types of dementia, which matters because treatments and disease courses can differ.

If your loved one has been diagnosed with early-onset dementia, consider seeking care at a memory or neurology center experienced with rare and genetic dementias, as these cases often require specialized expertise.

example_qa.q: My relative was first told they had Alzheimer's disease, but now doctors are talking about something called FTLD. How can the diagnosis change?
example_qa.a: It is more common than many people realize. Some forms of frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD) can cause memory or language problems that look very similar to Alzheimer's disease in early stages. As more information becomes available — such as brain scans, biomarker tests, or genetic results — doctors may refine the diagnosis. A changed diagnosis is not a mistake; it reflects doctors learning more about what is happening in your loved one's brain.

example_qa.q: Should our family consider genetic testing since our relative has this type of dementia?
example_qa.a: That is a very important question to raise with the medical team. Certain types of FTLD, including those linked to the GRN gene, can run in families. Genetic counseling can help your family understand the potential implications before deciding whether to pursue testing. A genetic counselor or specialist in hereditary dementias can guide you through this process in a sensitive way.

example_qa.q: Does it matter whether the diagnosis is FTLD or Alzheimer's disease if the symptoms look the same?
example_qa.a: The distinction can matter for several reasons. The underlying causes are different, the expected progression may differ, and the treatments being studied or used may vary. An accurate diagnosis also helps families understand the hereditary risk and access the most appropriate support services. It is worth discussing with the neurologist how the specific diagnosis affects your loved one's care plan.

summary_text: This 2026 Colombian case report describes two patients with frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD) caused by novel variants in the GRN (progranulin) gene, both of whom were initially misdiagnosed with Alzheimer's disease due to atypical presentations. Case 1, a 42-year-old, had prominent memory difficulties, while Case 2, a 62-year-old, experienced semantic (word-meaning) impairment — symptoms more commonly associated with AD than FTLD. Brain imaging showed asymmetric temporal lobe atrophy, and biomarker analysis helped confirm the FTLD diagnosis. The report highlights that GRN-related FTLD can convincingly mimic early-onset Alzheimer's disease, particularly in genetically diverse (admixed) populations like those in Latin America, where such variants have been undercharacterized. For caregivers, this case underscores the importance of comprehensive evaluation including genetic testing, brain imaging, and biomarkers when a loved one develops dementia at a young age or when the diagnosis seems uncertain. Consulting specialists experienced with hereditary and atypical dementias, and considering genetic counseling for the wider family, can be crucial steps toward accurate diagnosis and appropriate care planning.
title: Phenotypic diversity of frontotemporal lobar degeneration in two novel GRN variants from Colombia.

patient_profile: This case report describes a patient with early-onset, rapidly progressive frontotemporal dementia (FTD) caused by a novel genetic variant (MAPT P301A) in the tau protein gene. The patient's exact age and sex are not specified in the provided text, though the title indicates early onset. Key comorbidity is the genetic mutation itself, which accelerates tau pathology.
symptoms_behavior: The case involves rapidly progressive frontotemporal dementia symptoms. While specific behavioral symptoms (such as agitation, personality changes, or memory loss) are not detailed in the provided text excerpt, frontotemporal dementia typically presents with personality changes, language difficulties, and executive function problems rather than pure memory loss early on.
communication: Not detailed in the provided text excerpt.
progression: The title describes this as a rapidly progressive early-onset form of frontotemporal dementia linked to a novel MAPT gene variant. The laboratory research included in the text shows that tau protein can spread from cell to cell in a prion-like manner, which may help explain why some forms of dementia progress quickly. Specific clinical timeline for this patient is not detailed in the provided excerpt.
treatment_management: No specific treatments or medications for the patient are described in the provided text. The laboratory research focuses on understanding how tau protein spreads between brain cells, which is important for future therapeutic development. Currently, management of frontotemporal dementia is largely supportive and symptom-focused.
caregiver_insights: Frontotemporal dementia often causes personality and behavior changes before memory problems, which can be confusing and distressing for families — knowing this is a disease symptom, not a personal choice, can help caregivers respond with patience.
Rapidly progressive dementias can be emotionally overwhelming. Early planning for future care needs, legal matters, and support services is especially important when decline is fast.
If dementia runs in your family, genetic counseling may be available to discuss risks and options — ask your loved one's neurologist about this.
Because FTD can affect behavior and communication early, connecting with a social worker or dementia specialist who understands behavioral symptoms can provide practical coping strategies.

example_qa.q: My family member was diagnosed with frontotemporal dementia at a young age and seems to be getting worse very quickly. Is this normal?
example_qa.a: Some forms of frontotemporal dementia, especially those linked to genetic causes like changes in the MAPT gene, can progress more rapidly than typical Alzheimer's disease. Every person's experience is different. It's important to stay in close contact with your loved one's neurologist to monitor changes and adjust care plans as needed. Ask about referrals to a dementia specialist or a center with expertise in rapidly progressive dementias.

example_qa.q: What kinds of behavior changes should I expect with frontotemporal dementia?
example_qa.a: Frontotemporal dementia commonly causes changes in personality, social behavior, and language rather than memory loss early on. Your loved one may seem impulsive, withdrawn, emotionally flat, or say unusual things. These are symptoms of the disease affecting the frontal and temporal parts of the brain. A behavioral neurologist or neuropsychologist can help you understand what to expect and how to manage these changes safely.

example_qa.q: Is frontotemporal dementia genetic? Should other family members be tested?
example_qa.a: Some cases of frontotemporal dementia are caused by inherited gene changes, such as variants in the MAPT gene. If there is a known genetic cause in your family, other relatives may wish to speak with a genetic counselor about whether testing is appropriate for them. This is a personal decision and should be made with support from medical professionals who specialize in neurogenetics.

summary_text: This case concerns a patient with early-onset, rapidly progressive frontotemporal dementia caused by a novel variant in the MAPT gene (P301A), which affects the tau protein. While the clinical details of the patient are largely absent from the provided text excerpt — which is predominantly a laboratory research paper on how tau protein spreads between brain cells — the case highlights the genetic underpinnings of some aggressive dementias. Tau protein pathology, as shown in the laboratory work, can spread in a prion-like manner from cell to cell, potentially explaining rapid progression. For caregivers, frontotemporal dementia presents unique challenges including early personality and behavioral changes rather than memory loss, which can be difficult to understand and manage. Rapid progression calls for early care planning, connection with dementia specialists, and consideration of genetic counseling for family members. Supportive care, behavioral management strategies, and strong caregiver support networks are the cornerstones of management since no disease-modifying treatments currently exist.
title: Early onset rapidly progressive frontotemporal dementia due to a novel MAPT P301A variant with functional validation of pathogenicity.

patient_profile: A 54-year-old male (at time of case report writing) diagnosed with Early-Onset Alzheimer's Disease (EOAD) at age 47 in 2017. He was identified as a 'highly sensitive person' (HSP), meaning he had a temperament trait called sensory processing sensitivity — a heightened sensitivity to environmental stimuli and emotional experiences. No specific physical comorbidities are mentioned.
symptoms_behavior: Unlike typical late-onset Alzheimer's, this patient's early symptoms centered on executive function difficulties (planning, organizing, problem-solving), attention problems, and visual-perceptual impairments rather than prominent memory loss. Over six years, these deficits progressively affected his ability to manage daily tasks, maintain employment, and engage socially. His highly sensitive temperament likely made environmental changes and overstimulation particularly distressing.
communication: Not detailed in the case report, though the ecological and person-centered approach — including sessions held in his home and familiar environment — suggests communication was supported by keeping interactions in comfortable, familiar contexts.
progression: Diagnosed at age 47, the patient was followed neuropsychologically for 6 years. Early stages showed executive, attention, and visual-perceptual impairments. Functioning declined gradually across daily, occupational, and social domains. At age 59 (2022), he was admitted to a nursing home. His placement in an unfamiliar environment without personal belongings or autobiographical references appeared to accelerate deterioration markedly. He passed away at age 60 in 2023, approximately one year after nursing home admission.
treatment_management: The primary intervention was ongoing neuropsychological psychotherapy with a specialist in both neuropsychology and high sensitivity. Sessions were held twice weekly in the first year, then transitioned to an ecological approach — meaning sessions took place in the patient's home and natural daily environment. The framework used was person-centered care combined with the 'unmet needs model,' which focuses on identifying and meeting the patient's underlying emotional, psychological, and practical needs to reduce distress and support functioning. No specific medications are mentioned in the report.
caregiver_insights: Familiar environments matter enormously: This case illustrates how moving a person with dementia — especially someone who is highly sensitive — out of their familiar home environment can significantly speed up decline. Whenever possible, keeping your loved one in a known, comfortable setting with personal belongings and meaningful objects may help slow deterioration.

Know your loved one's temperament: If your family member has always been deeply affected by noise, crowds, emotions, or change, they may be a highly sensitive person. This trait can make dementia symptoms and distress more intense, and it means caregiving approaches need to be gentler, more predictable, and highly attuned to their sensory and emotional needs.

Person-centered care makes a difference: Working with professionals who treat the whole person — not just the diagnosis — and who tailor support to the individual's life story, preferences, and values can improve quality of life and potentially slow functional decline. Ask about neuropsychological support that uses this approach.

Early-onset Alzheimer's can look different: EOAD often presents with problems in planning, attention, and visual perception rather than memory loss first. If a younger family member (under 65) is showing these kinds of difficulties, advocate for thorough neuropsychological testing and differential diagnosis to ensure they receive the right support early.

example_qa.q: My husband has early-onset Alzheimer's and we're considering moving him to a memory care facility. Is that a bad idea?
example_qa.a: This case report highlights that a sudden move to an unfamiliar environment — away from personal belongings, familiar surroundings, and life memories — can be very stressful for someone with EOAD and may accelerate decline, especially if they are a sensitive person. That doesn't mean a care facility is always the wrong choice, but it's worth discussing with your care team how to make any transition as gradual and familiar as possible — bringing meaningful objects, photos, and personal items, and ensuring staff are briefed on your husband's life story and preferences. A person-centered approach in any setting can make a real difference.

example_qa.q: My mother was always very sensitive to noise, emotions, and change. Now she has dementia. Should I manage her care differently than I would for someone who isn't like that?
example_qa.a: Yes, absolutely. People with a highly sensitive temperament tend to be more deeply affected by their environment, sensory input, and emotional atmosphere. For someone like your mother, keeping routines calm and predictable, reducing background noise and overstimulation, and maintaining familiar surroundings can be especially important. It's also worth looking for a neuropsychologist or therapist who understands both dementia and high sensitivity, as they can tailor communication and support strategies to her specific needs.

example_qa.q: My brother was diagnosed with Alzheimer's at age 50 and his main problems seem to be with planning and seeing things clearly, not really his memory. Is that normal for Alzheimer's?
example_qa.a: Early-onset Alzheimer's disease can indeed look quite different from the late-onset form many people are familiar with. In younger people, it often first affects executive functions like planning and organizing, attention, and visual-perceptual abilities, rather than episodic memory. This can make it harder to diagnose at first, as it may be confused with other conditions. It's really important to have a thorough neuropsychological evaluation by a specialist experienced with EOAD, so the right support and treatment plan can be put in place as early as possible.

summary_text: This 2025 case report follows a 54-year-old highly sensitive male diagnosed with Early-Onset Alzheimer's Disease (EOAD) at age 47, who was tracked neuropsychologically for six years until his death at age 60. Unlike typical Alzheimer's presentations, his symptoms primarily affected executive functioning, attention, and visual perception rather than memory. His temperament — characterized by heightened sensory processing sensitivity — made environmental changes and overstimulation particularly impactful on his wellbeing. He received ongoing person-centered neuropsychological therapy in his home environment, using the unmet needs model to address cognitive, emotional, and functional challenges. A critical finding was that his placement in a nursing home at age 59, away from familiar surroundings and personal life references, appeared to dramatically accelerate his decline, and he passed away approximately one year later. For caregivers, this case underscores the profound importance of familiar environments, individualized person-centered care, understanding a loved one's unique temperament, and seeking specialized neuropsychological support. It also serves as a reminder that EOAD can present atypically, and early, thorough assessment is essential for quality of life and appropriate management.
title: Highly sensitive early-onset Alzheimer's disease: a case report.

patient_profile: A 33-year-old woman with no significant prior medical history who developed early-onset Alzheimer's disease. This is considered an atypical presentation because of her very young age (most early-onset AD occurs between ages 40–65). No relevant family history or genetic findings were reported.
symptoms_behavior: Over a two-year period she experienced a progressive decline in multiple areas of thinking and function. Key symptoms included memory and cognitive difficulties severe enough to cause job loss, dangerous lapses in judgment (such as cooking fires left unattended), impaired attention, involuntary muscle jerks (myoclonus), overactive reflexes (hyperreflexia), and an unsteady, poorly coordinated walk (dystaxic gait). Both memory and physical/motor abilities were affected.
communication: Not detailed. The case report does not describe specific changes in her language or speech abilities.
progression: The decline unfolded over approximately two years before diagnosis. She went from functioning independently and holding a job to losing employment and being unable to safely manage everyday tasks like cooking. Brain imaging showed cortical (outer brain) shrinkage and reduced energy use in the parietal region, which is involved in spatial awareness and coordination. The case was still in the diagnostic and treatment-planning phase at the time of writing.
treatment_management: A thorough workup was completed, including brain MRI, FDG-PET scan, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis, genetic testing, autoimmune screening, and metabolic labs — most of which came back normal or with only minor findings. She was referred to a specialized memory center for further evaluation and was being considered for treatment with lecanemab, a newer antibody therapy targeting amyloid plaques. No other specific medications or therapies were detailed in the report.
caregiver_insights: Early-onset AD can appear in people in their 30s or 40s — a diagnosis is not limited to older adults. If a younger family member shows persistent cognitive decline, advocate strongly for a full neurological evaluation even if doctors initially seem skeptical.

Everyday safety is a real and urgent concern. Cooking fires and similar incidents in this case highlight the need for caregivers to assess the home environment early and put safety measures in place (supervised cooking, stove safety devices, etc.).

Diagnosis can take time and involve many tests. A normal blood test or even a normal spinal fluid test does not automatically rule out Alzheimer's — advanced imaging like MRI and PET scans may be needed. Stay persistent and seek referral to a memory specialist or center.

Newer treatments like lecanemab are emerging and may be options for some patients, particularly those identified early. Asking the neurologist about eligibility for newer therapies or clinical trials is worthwhile.

example_qa.q: My family member is only in her 30s. Can someone that young really have Alzheimer's disease?
example_qa.a: Yes, though it is uncommon. Early-onset Alzheimer's disease can occur before age 65, and in rare cases even in a person's 30s, as this case report shows. If your family member is showing a consistent, worsening decline in memory, thinking, or day-to-day function, it is important to seek evaluation from a neurologist or memory specialist, regardless of their age.

example_qa.q: The doctors ran a lot of tests and most came back normal. Does that mean it isn't Alzheimer's?
example_qa.a: Not necessarily. As this case illustrates, many standard tests — including spinal fluid, genetic, and autoimmune workups — can come back normal even when Alzheimer's is present. Advanced brain imaging such as MRI or PET scans may reveal changes that point toward a diagnosis. A referral to a specialized memory center can be an important next step when routine tests are inconclusive.

example_qa.q: What can I do at home to keep my loved one safe while we wait for a diagnosis or treatment plan?
example_qa.a: Safety in the home is a priority from the moment you notice significant cognitive changes. Simple steps include never leaving your loved one alone while cooking, using stove knob covers or automatic shut-off devices, removing trip hazards, and establishing daily routines. It is also helpful to discuss driving safety with the medical team. You do not need a final diagnosis to start making the home safer — begin as soon as you see concerning behaviors.

summary_text: This 2025 case report describes a 33-year-old woman with no prior medical history who developed atypical early-onset Alzheimer's disease over a two-year period. Her symptoms included significant cognitive decline across memory and executive function, job loss, dangerous lapses such as cooking fires, involuntary muscle jerks, overactive reflexes, and an unsteady gait. Standard blood, genetic, autoimmune, and cerebrospinal fluid tests were largely normal, but brain MRI and FDG-PET imaging revealed cortical atrophy and reduced metabolic activity in the parietal region. After an extensive diagnostic workup, she was referred to a memory center and considered for lecanemab therapy. The case underscores that early-onset AD can occur in very young adults, may mimic other conditions, and requires advanced imaging and specialist referral for accurate diagnosis. For caregivers, this report highlights the importance of home safety interventions early in the disease course, persistence in seeking specialized care even when initial tests are normal, and awareness that emerging treatments may be available for patients identified at an early stage.
title: Atypical Early Onset Alzheimer's Disease in a Young Female: A Case Report.

patient_profile: 61-year-old woman with a diagnosis of Alzheimer's Disease (AD), presenting alongside a rare movement disorder called functional propriospinal myoclonus (PSM). No additional comorbidities are detailed beyond anxiety and restlessness mentioned in the context of her symptoms.
symptoms_behavior: The patient experienced involuntary, arrhythmic (irregular) trunk movements — a movement disorder layered on top of her Alzheimer's diagnosis. She also showed notable anxiety and restlessness. Importantly, the trunk movements resolved when she was distracted, which is a hallmark clue that helped clinicians identify the functional (rather than purely structural) nature of her movement symptoms.
communication: Not detailed in this case report.
progression: Not detailed extensively. The case focuses on a specific point in time when the movement disorder was identified and evaluated. The coexistence of Alzheimer's disease with a functional movement disorder was noted as rare and newly described. Treatment with Sertraline led to improvement in both the motor symptoms and anxiety, suggesting a positive short-term response.
treatment_management: The patient was treated with Sertraline (an antidepressant also used for anxiety), which improved both her involuntary trunk movements and her anxiety symptoms. The case emphasizes personalized, integrated management — meaning treatment was tailored to address both the neurological and emotional/behavioral dimensions of her condition. Electrophysiological testing (brain signal monitoring) was used to confirm the functional diagnosis.
caregiver_insights: Unusual movements in a loved one with Alzheimer's — such as repetitive trunk jerking — are worth reporting promptly to their doctor, as they may signal an additional condition that can be treated separately from dementia itself.
Anxiety and restlessness in someone with Alzheimer's can sometimes drive or worsen physical symptoms like involuntary movements. Addressing emotional wellbeing may help reduce physical symptoms too.

Distraction techniques (redirecting attention) may naturally reduce certain functional movement symptoms, as was observed in this patient. Caregivers can note whether movements ease when the person is engaged in a calming or absorbing activity, and share this observation with clinicians.

People with Alzheimer's can develop additional neurological or psychiatric conditions that require their own diagnosis and treatment. Caregivers should advocate for thorough evaluation if new or changing symptoms appear, rather than assuming everything is part of the dementia.

example_qa.q: My mother with Alzheimer's has started making sudden jerking movements with her trunk. Could this be part of her dementia?
example_qa.a: Jerking or involuntary movements can sometimes occur in Alzheimer's, but they can also be signs of a separate condition, as described in at least one reported case. It's really important to tell her doctor right away so the movements can be properly evaluated. A specialist may use tests to figure out the cause and find the right treatment.

example_qa.q: The doctor mentioned a 'functional movement disorder' alongside my loved one's Alzheimer's. What does 'functional' mean?
example_qa.a: 'Functional' means the brain's circuits are not working in the usual coordinated way, even though there isn't a new structural injury or lesion causing it. It doesn't mean the symptoms aren't real — they very much are. These disorders can often improve with the right treatment, such as certain medications or therapies targeting mood and anxiety, as was seen in this reported case.

example_qa.q: Could anxiety be making my family member's physical symptoms worse?
example_qa.a: Yes, anxiety can interact with and worsen certain movement or physical symptoms in people with dementia. In the case described, treating anxiety with medication also helped improve the patient's involuntary movements. Sharing any signs of anxiety or restlessness with the care team is a good idea, as addressing emotional health can sometimes have a positive effect on physical symptoms too.

summary_text: This 2025 case report describes a 61-year-old woman with Alzheimer's disease who developed a rare functional movement disorder called propriospinal myoclonus — presenting as involuntary, irregular trunk jerking accompanied by anxiety and restlessness. Her movements notably calmed when she was distracted, a key diagnostic clue. Specialized electrophysiological testing confirmed the functional nature of her condition. She was treated with Sertraline, which improved both her movement symptoms and anxiety, highlighting how personalized, integrated treatment can address overlapping neurological and emotional challenges in people with dementia. For family caregivers, this case is a reminder to report any new or unusual physical symptoms — especially sudden movements — to the medical team promptly, to note whether redirection or distraction helps, and to recognize that anxiety and emotional distress in a loved one with Alzheimer's may contribute to physical symptoms. People with Alzheimer's can develop additional conditions beyond dementia that deserve and respond to their own specific treatment.
title: Functional propriospinal myoclonus in Alzheimer's disease: coincidence or a new challenge?

patient_profile: An older adult with Alzheimer's disease (AD) complicated by behavioral and psychological symptoms of dementia (BPSD). The patient had a poor response to standard drug treatments. Specific age and sex are not detailed in the abstract, but the case involves established dementia with significant behavioral complications.
symptoms_behavior: The patient experienced significant behavioral and psychological symptoms of dementia (BPSD), which may include agitation, mood disturbances, and mental behavior disorder. Cognitive impairment was also present. Sleep disturbances were noted, including prolonged sleep duration as an adverse effect of one treatment setting.
communication: Not detailed in this case report.
progression: The case describes an established dementia patient with BPSD who had already failed standard drug treatments. The timeline covers approximately one month of initial rTMS treatment followed by adjustments. Over the course of treatment, cognitive function fluctuated depending on the stimulation parameters used, ultimately stabilizing with a personalized low-frequency approach.
treatment_management: The patient was treated with repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS), a non-invasive brain stimulation technique, after poor response to medications. Three different frequency settings were tried: 1 Hz rTMS improved behavioral symptoms but worsened cognitive function and caused excessive sleep. 10 Hz rTMS improved both cognition and behavior but triggered a seizure. 0.8 Hz rTMS ultimately provided symptom improvement without seizures. This case highlights that rTMS requires careful, individualized adjustment by medical professionals.
caregiver_insights: rTMS is a non-drug option being explored for dementia-related behavioral symptoms when medications are not working well, but it requires close medical supervision due to possible side effects like sleep changes or, rarely, seizures.

Behavioral and psychological symptoms of dementia (BPSD) — such as agitation or mood problems — can sometimes be addressed with non-medication approaches, and it is worth asking the care team about all available options.

Treatment adjustments may be needed over time. What works at one setting or dose may need to be fine-tuned, so caregivers should monitor and report any new or worsening symptoms to the medical team promptly.

If your loved one has not responded well to medications for behavioral symptoms, discuss with their doctor whether other interventions like rTMS might be appropriate and available at a specialist center.

example_qa.q: What is rTMS and could it help my family member with dementia who is very agitated and not responding to medications?
example_qa.a: Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) is a non-invasive procedure that uses magnetic pulses to gently stimulate specific areas of the brain. Some research, including this case, suggests it may help reduce behavioral symptoms like agitation in people with Alzheimer's disease, especially when medications haven't worked well. However, it needs to be done in a medical setting with careful monitoring, as the settings need to be individualized. Talk to your loved one's neurologist or dementia specialist to see if it might be an option.

example_qa.q: Are there side effects from rTMS that I should watch out for as a caregiver?
example_qa.a: Yes, this case report shows that side effects can happen and depend on the specific settings used. The patient experienced worsened cognitive function and longer-than-normal sleep at one setting, and had a seizure at another. The good news is that with careful adjustment by the medical team, a safer setting was found that helped without causing these problems. As a caregiver, report any unusual sleepiness, confusion, or other changes to the doctor right away after any rTMS session.

example_qa.q: My mother's dementia symptoms keep changing. How do doctors decide which treatment to try?
example_qa.a: Managing dementia symptoms often involves trial and careful adjustment, as every person responds differently. Doctors consider the type and stage of dementia, which symptoms are most troublesome, and how the person has responded to previous treatments. This case is a good example of how a medical team may try different approaches — including adjusting the frequency of a treatment like rTMS — until they find what works best for that individual. Keeping a simple diary of your loved one's daily symptoms, sleep, and mood can be very helpful information to share with the care team.

summary_text: This 2023 case report describes an Alzheimer's disease patient with significant behavioral and psychological symptoms of dementia (BPSD) who did not respond adequately to standard medications. The care team tried repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS), a non-invasive brain stimulation therapy, using three different frequency settings over time. The first setting (1 Hz) improved behavior but worsened cognition and caused excessive sleep. A higher setting (10 Hz) improved both cognition and behavior but triggered a seizure. A personalized lower setting (0.8 Hz) ultimately provided meaningful symptom relief without serious side effects. For caregivers, this case illustrates that when medications fall short, specialist teams may explore non-drug brain stimulation approaches for behavioral symptoms, but these require expert supervision and individualized adjustment. Caregivers play a vital role by closely observing and reporting any changes in sleep, alertness, or behavior to the medical team so treatment can be safely optimized.
title: The repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation in Alzheimer's disease patients with behavioral and psychological symptoms of dementia: a case report.

patient_profile: A 52-year-old individual (sex not specified in the text) diagnosed with early-onset Alzheimer's disease presenting as Posterior Cortical Atrophy (PCA). The patient carried a rare genetic variant in the PSEN1 gene, which is linked to familial, early-onset Alzheimer's disease. No other comorbidities were mentioned.
symptoms_behavior: The patient's main symptoms were progressive difficulty with visuospatial tasks (trouble understanding or navigating visual space) and apraxia (difficulty performing coordinated movements or tasks despite physical ability). These are characteristic of Posterior Cortical Atrophy, a less common form of Alzheimer's where vision and spatial processing are affected earlier and more prominently than memory.
communication: Not detailed in this case report. However, PCA typically preserves language and memory relatively early on, while visual and spatial abilities decline first.
progression: The patient was 52 years old at the time of diagnosis, placing this firmly in the early-onset category. The disorder was described as progressive. A cerebrospinal fluid biomarker test confirmed Alzheimer's disease pathology, and genetic testing identified a PSEN1 mutation that likely drove the early onset. The full timeline of progression was not detailed.
treatment_management: No specific medications or therapies were described in this case. Management in confirmed PSEN1-related early-onset AD typically involves specialist neurological care, genetic counseling for family members, and supportive therapies for the specific symptoms present (such as occupational therapy for apraxia and visuospatial difficulties). Caregivers should work closely with a neurologist experienced in early-onset and genetic dementias.
caregiver_insights: PCA affects vision and spatial skills first — your loved one may struggle to recognize objects, judge distances, or perform familiar tasks, even though their memory may seem relatively intact early on. This is still Alzheimer's disease, just starting in a different part of the brain.

Because the person is only 52, they may still appear physically healthy and capable, which can make it harder for others to understand the diagnosis. Connecting with early-onset dementia support groups can be very helpful for both the person and their caregiver.
A PSEN1 genetic variant means this form of Alzheimer's is hereditary. Consider encouraging other family members to speak with a genetic counselor to understand their own risk and options.

Occupational therapy can be particularly valuable for someone with apraxia and visuospatial problems — therapists can suggest home adaptations and strategies to keep the person safer and more independent for longer.

example_qa.q: My spouse was diagnosed with Posterior Cortical Atrophy at age 52. Why do they struggle so much with vision and doing tasks, but can still remember conversations?
example_qa.a: Posterior Cortical Atrophy is a form of Alzheimer's disease that primarily affects the back part of the brain, which handles vision, spatial awareness, and coordinated movements. This is why your spouse may have trouble recognizing objects, navigating spaces, or performing familiar tasks — while memory and conversation may be less affected in the earlier stages. It is still Alzheimer's disease, just with a different starting point.

example_qa.q: We found out my parent has a PSEN1 gene mutation. Should the rest of our family get tested?
example_qa.a: This is an important and very personal decision. A PSEN1 mutation can be inherited, and other family members may want to speak with a genetic counselor who specializes in hereditary dementia. A counselor can explain the chances of inheriting the variant, what testing involves emotionally and practically, and what options exist. There is no pressure to test, and the decision is entirely up to each individual.

example_qa.q: How can I help my loved one at home when they struggle to do everyday tasks because of their PCA?
example_qa.a: Helping someone with apraxia and visuospatial difficulties takes patience and creativity. Breaking tasks into small, simple steps can make them more manageable. Reducing clutter, improving lighting, and using contrasting colors (like a brightly colored cup on a plain surface) can help with visual challenges. An occupational therapist can assess your home and suggest practical adaptations tailored to your loved one's specific needs. Always consult with their care team for personalized advice.

summary_text: This 2023 case report describes a 52-year-old with early-onset Alzheimer's disease presenting as Posterior Cortical Atrophy (PCA), caused by a rare PSEN1 genetic variant. The patient's key symptoms were progressive visuospatial impairment and apraxia — difficulties with spatial understanding and performing coordinated tasks — rather than the memory loss typically associated with Alzheimer's. Diagnosis was confirmed using neuropsychological testing, brain imaging, cerebrospinal fluid biomarkers, and genetic sequencing. For family caregivers, this case highlights that Alzheimer's can look very different depending on which brain regions are affected first. Caregivers of someone with PCA may find that their loved one struggles with vision-related tasks and physical coordination while remaining conversationally coherent early in the disease. The hereditary nature of PSEN1 mutations makes genetic counseling an important consideration for the wider family. Supportive strategies such as occupational therapy, home modifications, and connection with early-onset dementia networks can meaningfully improve quality of life.
title: A Novel PSEN1 Variant Leading to Posterior Cortical Atrophy: A Case Report.

patient_profile: A 59-year-old woman with early-onset Alzheimer's disease (EOAD). Her symptoms first appeared at age 46, she was diagnosed with depression at age 50, and cognitive decline became apparent at age 53. The case was followed for 9 years. Key features include early onset (before age 65) and an initial presentation that closely resembled a mood disorder rather than a memory condition.
symptoms_behavior: Her first noticeable symptoms were depression-related — low mood and emotional changes — starting in her mid-40s. Memory loss and disorientation emerged several years later, around age 53. Over time, these cognitive symptoms worsened progressively until she met the full criteria for dementia. The case highlights how early-onset Alzheimer's can look like depression first, which can delay the correct diagnosis.
communication: Not detailed in this report. However, given her progression from mild cognitive symptoms to dementia over several years, communication difficulties would be expected to have developed gradually.
progression: The disease followed a slow but steady course over roughly 13 years from first symptoms to confirmed dementia. Depression appeared first (around age 46–50), memory and orientation problems followed (age 53), and dementia was eventually confirmed. Brain scans taken over time showed the hippocampus (the brain's memory center) shrinking year by year, and widespread thinning of the outer brain layers. Standardized memory tests (MMSE and MoCA) declined steadily each year until scores fell into the dementia range.
treatment_management: The report does not detail specific medications used. Management emphasized careful monitoring using neuropsychological tests (MMSE and MoCA scores tracked annually) and advanced brain imaging — MRI to track brain shrinkage, FDG-PET to detect reduced brain activity, and amyloid PET (AV45) to confirm Alzheimer's-related protein deposits. The case underscores the importance of combining mood assessment tools with brain imaging for earlier, more accurate diagnosis in people who present with depression first.
caregiver_insights: Depression can be an early sign of Alzheimer's — if a loved one in their 40s or 50s develops depression alongside subtle memory or orientation changes, it is worth asking their doctor whether a full cognitive evaluation (including brain imaging) might be appropriate.

Early-onset Alzheimer's (before age 65) is often misdiagnosed initially because symptoms like depression are more commonly linked to mood disorders. Persistence in seeking a thorough evaluation can make a real difference in getting the right diagnosis sooner.

Regular cognitive testing (such as MMSE or MoCA) done year after year can help track changes over time. If scores decline steadily, this is an important signal to discuss with a neurologist or memory specialist.
